props.title: Theorem

sections.content: Theorem stands as Pier Paolo Pasolini's most enigmatic and provocative work, starring Terence Stamp as a mysterious stranger who systematically seduces every member of an upper-class Milanese family. The film's clinical approach to sexuality and class destruction influenced later works like The Servant (1963) and Teorema (2004), which similarly explore power dynamics through intimate invasion. Pasolini's bold mixing of Catholic imagery with Marxist critique created a template for politically-charged arthouse cinema that echoes through films like The Cook, the Thief, His Wife & Her Lover (1989).

sections.content: The film's influence on European art cinema cannot be overstated. Its combination of bourgeois critique and religious allegory created a new vocabulary for political filmmaking. Directors like Fassbinder picked up Pasolini's thread in works like Fox and His Friends (1975) and The Bitter Tears of Petra von Kant (1972), using sexuality as a lens to examine class warfare. The stranger's divine/demonic nature prefigured similar mysterious catalysts in films like Visitor Q (2001) and Swept Away (1974).

Pasolini's formal techniques in Theorem - the long silences, static compositions, and sudden bursts of handheld camera - established a visual language for depicting spiritual crisis that influenced filmmakers from Tarkovsky to von Trier. The film's ending, with its famous levitation scene and descent into madness, opened new possibilities for mixing realism with symbolic imagery. SUBHEAD: Sexual Politics and Class Critique

sections.content: The film's systematic deconstruction of family structures through sexuality created ripples through European cinema, particularly in the works of Catherine Breillat like Romance (1999) and Fat Girl (2001). The way Theorem uses eroticism as a weapon against bourgeois complacency influenced filmmakers like Nagisa Oshima in works like In the Realm of the Senses (1976) and Empire of Passion (1978).
